sentences.text: Edaphodon was a member of the order Chimaeriformes, a group of cartilaginous fish related to sharks and rays, belonging to the class Chondrichthyes.
The type species of the genus is Edaphodon bucklandii, and it is classified in the family Callorhinchidae, though it is sometimes assigned to the family Edaphodontidae.
Some species of Edaphodon, such as E. mirificus, reached lengths of over 3 meters, with one individual estimated at 3.43 meters.
The largest mandibular tooth plates of E. sedgwickii reached 225 mm, while those of E. snowhillensis reached 180 mm.
The genus Edaphodon was first described by William Buckland in 1838.
There are 65 recorded fossil occurrences of Edaphodon in the Paleobiology Database.
Edaphodon fed using six pairs of tooth plates bearing hypermineralized areas called tritors, located on the lower jaw and two upper jaw plates.

Edaphodon's tooth plates had distinct patterns: vomerine plates had rod-like tritors, palatine plates had one large outer tritor with pads in the center, and mandibular plates had a beak-like tritor with pads at the edges and center.
Edaphodon likely used its tritors to crush hard-shelled prey and slice fish, sharks, and marine reptiles.
Edaphodon first appeared in the Aptian age of the Lower Cretaceous and went extinct during the Pliocene, living from the Aptian to the Zanclean stages, spanning from 119.57 to 3.6 million years ago.
The genus was most prominent during the Late Cretaceous period, and its species were found in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, including New Zealand and Antarctica.
